title: Chinese Sausage Fried Rice
subtitle: lap cheong sausage with egg fried rice and soy
excerpt: Day-old jasmine rice stir-fried at high heat with sweet-smoky Chinese sausage, scrambled egg, spring onions and a splash of light soy. A Cantonese comfort dish ready in 25 minutes. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Lap cheong (Chinese dried sausage) fried rice is a mainstay of Cantonese home cooking. Lap cheong has been made in China for centuries; early cured sausage methods are documented in Chinese agricultural texts from the Han dynasty. The use of dried sausage in fried rice became widespread as a practical way to extend the flavour of a small amount of preserved meat across a pot of rice. The dish appears in Cantonese cookbooks throughout the twentieth century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cold, day-old rice is essential. Spread freshly cooked rice on a tray and refrigerate uncovered overnight if you do not have leftovers.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dried, cured pork sausages (lap cheong in Cantonese) with a sweet, smoky flavour and reddish colour from soy sauce and rice wine. Sold in vacuum-packed pairs in Asian grocery shops. They must be cooked before eating, which can be done by slicing and pan-frying or steaming.

Literally 'breath of the wok'. The slightly smoky, charred aroma that develops when food is cooked over very high heat in a well-seasoned wok. Achieved at home by getting the wok as hot as possible before adding oil.

A thin, salty soy sauce used for seasoning. It is lighter in colour than dark soy sauce but stronger in saltiness. Standard for fried rice, dressings and dipping sauces. Not to be confused with low-sodium soy sauce.

A dark, fragrant oil pressed from toasted sesame seeds. Used as a finishing condiment rather than a cooking oil, as its flavour diminishes under direct heat. A small amount adds a characteristic nutty aroma.

content.text: This dish takes 25 minutes and serves 4.
Chinese sausage
is sliced and fried until caramelised, then cold day-old rice goes into the same wok for
wok hei
. It is seasoned simply with
light soy sauce
and finished with a drizzle of
sesame oil
Day-old rice is not optional. Freshly cooked rice has too much steam and moisture; it clumps rather than fries. Break up the cold rice with your hands before it goes into the wok.
What you need
Method
Break the cold rice apart with damp hands to separate the grains. Set aside.
Heat the wok over high heat until smoking. Add 1 tbsp oil. Fry the sausage slices for 2 minutes, stirring, until caramelised and slightly charred at the edges. Remove and set aside.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil. Add the garlic and stir for 20 seconds.
Push the garlic to one side. Pour in the beaten eggs and scramble until just set.
Add the rice. Press it against the wok with a spatula and toss vigorously for 2 to 3 minutes over high heat, breaking up any clumps.
Return the sausage to the wok. Add the soy sauce, white pepper and spring onions. Toss for 1 more minute.
Remove from the heat, drizzle with sesame oil and serve immediately.

items.cause: Freshly cooked rice was used, or it was not broken up before frying.
items.fix: Use rice that has been refrigerated overnight and break it apart before it goes into the wok.

items.cause: Not cooked long enough to render the fat.
items.fix: Fry the sausage slices for 2 full minutes over high heat until the edges colour. The fat should look translucent.

items.cause: It was left in the wok too long before the rice was added.
items.fix: Add the rice as soon as the egg is just set. The residual heat from the rice will finish cooking the egg.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Chinese sausage fried rice is Cantonese comfort food at its simplest. Lap cheong is a pantry staple in southern Chinese households and across South-East Asian Chinese communities, eaten steamed over rice, sliced into clay pot dishes, or stir-fried. Its high fat and sugar content means it caramelises quickly in a hot wok, leaving a sweetness in the rice that no fresh ingredient quite replicates.
